title: Bayes on a trading signal
objectives: Decide how far a signal with a known detection rate should move your view
Combine a signal with a base rate and with other independent evidence
Size a bet from the posterior, and discount correlated signals

screens.prose: A trading signal flashes before some days. In years of data it flashed before 60% of up days and before 40% of down days. Up and down days were equally common.
screens.question: The signal flashes today. What is the chance today is an up day?

widget.label: Chance of an up day given a flash

hints.text: Keep only the paths where the signal flashes.
Two paths end in a flash.
Up and flash: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{3}{5} = 0.3$. Down and flash: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{2}{5} = 0.2$. The chance is $\tfrac{0.3}{0.5}$.

feedback.correct: 0.3 of the 0.5 that flash are up days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the up-and-flash path by both flash paths.

byKey.joint: That is $P(\text{up and flash})$. Divide it by the chance of a flash, 0.5.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the signal. The flash is evidence: use it.

explain.text: $P(\text{up} \mid \text{flash}) = \tfrac{0.3}{0.3 + 0.2} = 0.6$: the share of flashes that were right, which desks call the **hit rate**. It equals the 60% **detection rate**, $P(\text{flash} \mid \text{up})$, only because the prior is 50–50 and false alarms are 40%. Change either and the two numbers part.

screens.prose: Keep the false-alarm rate at 40% of down days. Slide the detection rate and the prior, and watch the view before and after a flash.

derive.caption: Likelihood ratio {{fixed(h / 0.4, 2)}}: the view moves from {{fixed(pr, 2)}} to {{fixed(pr * h / (pr * h + (1 - pr) * 0.4), 3)}}

screens.question: Keep the prior at 50%. Which detection rate leaves the view exactly where it was?

options.why: At 50% the signal still flashes more on up days than on down days, 0.5 against 0.4, so it moves the view to 0.556.
At 60% the view moves from 0.5 to 0.6. Slide lower.

options.text: None: every signal moves the view
options.why: Slide the detection rate down to the false-alarm rate and watch the two bars meet.

hints.text: Watch the two bars as you slide the detection rate.
The false-alarm rate is fixed at 40%.
When the detection rate equals the false-alarm rate, the likelihood ratio is 1.

feedback.correct: A detection rate equal to the false-alarm rate tells you nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the detection rate until the two bars are level.

explain.text: At a 40% detection rate the signal flashes as often on down days as on up days. Its likelihood ratio is $\tfrac{0.4}{0.4} = 1$, so the view does not move. A detection rate means something only next to the false-alarm rate.

screens.prose: In odds form, a flash multiplies the odds of an up day by the **likelihood ratio** $\dfrac{P(\text{flash} \mid \text{up})}{P(\text{flash} \mid \text{down})}$.
screens.question: What is the likelihood ratio of a flash for our signal?

hints.text: Divide the detection rate by the false-alarm rate.
The two flash branches carry 3/5 and 2/5.

feedback.correct: A flash is 1.5 times as likely on an up day as on a down day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the up-day flash rate on top and the down-day flash rate below.

byKey.flip: You put the false-alarm rate on top. The ratio for up against down puts 0.6 on top.
byKey.diff: You subtracted the rates. The likelihood ratio divides them.
byKey.hit: That is the detection rate alone. Divide it by the false-alarm rate.

explain.text: $\text{LR} = \tfrac{0.6}{0.4} = 1.5$. From even odds, 1 to 1, a flash gives odds 1.5 to 1, which is the 0.6 we found. Every use of this signal is now one multiplication.

screens.prose: Over the years, 55% of days were up days, not 50%. The signal is the same: it flashes before 60% of up days and 40% of down days.
screens.question: The signal flashes. What is the chance today is an up day?

widget.label: Chance of an up day given a flash

hints.text: Turn the prior into odds first.
Prior odds are $\tfrac{0.55}{0.45} = \tfrac{11}{9}$.
Posterior odds $\tfrac{11}{9} \times 1.5 = \tfrac{11}{6} \approx 1.833$. Then $p = \tfrac{1.833}{2.833}$.

feedback.correct: Odds of 11 to 6, a chance of about 0.647.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds, not the prior chance, by 1.5.

byKey.even: You kept the 50–50 prior. Up days are 55% of days, so start from odds of 11 to 9.
byKey.prior: That is the base rate before the flash. The flash should move it.
byKey.prob: You multiplied the probability 0.55 by 1.5. The likelihood ratio multiplies odds, not probabilities.
byKey.odds: That is the posterior odds, 11 to 6. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{11}{11 + 6}$.

explain.text: Odds $\tfrac{55}{45} \times 1.5 = 1.8333$, so $p = \tfrac{1.8333}{2.8333} = \tfrac{11}{17} \approx 0.6471$. The same flash lands higher because the view started higher. Always start from the base rate of up days.

screens.prose: Back to a 50% prior. Two different signals, each with a likelihood ratio of 1.5, are built from unrelated data. Given the day’s direction, they flash independently. Both flash today.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

widget.label: Chance of an up day given two flashes

hints.text: Each independent flash multiplies the odds by 1.5.
Two flashes multiply the odds by $1.5^2$.

feedback.correct: Two independent flashes take the odds to 2.25.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 1.5 once per independent flash.

byKey.one: You used only one flash. The second is independent evidence, so multiply by 1.5 again.
byKey.add: You added 0.1 per flash. Evidence multiplies odds; it does not add to probabilities.
byKey.odds: That is the posterior odds. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{2.25}{1 + 2.25}$.

explain.text: Odds $1.5^2 = 2.25$, so $p = \tfrac{2.25}{3.25} = \tfrac{9}{13} \approx 0.692$. The multiplication is valid only because the signals are independent given the day. The next screen breaks that.

screens.prose: Edge case. A second signal is the first one’s indicator, lightly smoothed. In the data it flashes on exactly the same days as the first. Both flash today.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

options.why: You multiplied by 1.5 twice. The second signal copies the first, so its flash adds no new evidence.
Agreement between copies is guaranteed. It tells you nothing new about the day.

hints.text: Given the first flash, how likely is the second?
The second flashes whenever the first does, on up and down days alike.
Its likelihood ratio, given the first, is $\tfrac{1}{1} = 1$.

feedback.correct: A copy of a signal counts once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the second flash adds once you have seen the first.

explain.text: Given the first flash, the second flashes for certain on up and down days alike: a likelihood ratio of 1. So the view stays at 0.6. Correlated signals count as fewer, and a perfect copy counts as none.

screens.prose: A vendor sells a signal with a “60% detection rate”: it flashes before 60% of up days. The small print says it also flashes before 60% of down days. Up days are 55% of days.
screens.question: The signal flashes. What is the chance today is an up day?

options.why: You took the detection rate as the probability of an up day. The detection rate is $P(\text{flash} \mid \text{up})$; you need $P(\text{up} \mid \text{flash})$.
That uses a 40% false-alarm rate. This signal flashes on 60% of down days.
You multiplied 0.55 by 1.5. The likelihood ratio here is $\tfrac{0.6}{0.6} = 1$.

hints.text: Compare how often it flashes on up days and on down days.
Both flash branches carry 3/5.
The likelihood ratio is $\tfrac{0.6}{0.6} = 1$, so the view stays at the base rate.

feedback.correct: A signal that flashes equally on up and down days is worthless.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the likelihood ratio before you use the detection rate.

byKey.hit: You took the detection rate as the probability of an up day. A 60% detection rate with 60% false alarms gives a likelihood ratio of 1.

explain.text: The signal flashes on 60% of days whatever the direction, so its likelihood ratio is 1. $P(\text{up} \mid \text{flash}) = 0.55$, the base rate. A detection rate quoted without its false-alarm rate tells you nothing.

screens.prose: From a 50% prior, how many independent flashes of our signal does it take to be at least 80% sure of an up day?
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: After $n$ independent flashes, odds $= 1 \times 1.5^n$, one factor of 1.5 per flash
We need $1.5^n \ge 4$, since 80% is odds of $\dfrac{0.8}{0.2} = 4$
So $n = 4$: three flashes give 0.771, four give 0.835

hints.text: Start from the odds before any flash.
The condition on $1.5^n$ needs the odds after $n$ flashes first.
Prior odds, odds after $n$ flashes, the target of 4, take logs, round up.

feedback.correct: Four flashes are the fewest that clear 80%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the prior odds and multiply once per flash.

byKey.need: The target is a condition on the odds after $n$ flashes, so that line comes first.
byKey.four: Rounding up comes after taking logs, so it is last.

explain.text: $\ln 4 / \ln 1.5 = 1.386 / 0.405 \approx 3.42$, so 3 flashes fall short and 4 suffice. Three give odds 3.375, a chance of 0.771; four give odds 5.06, a chance of 0.835. This holds only if the flashes really are independent.

screens.prose: After a flash the posterior chance of an up day is 0.6. You can make an even-money bet on it, win or lose the stake, many times over. With $p$ and the odds known, the Kelly rule stakes $2p - 1$ of capital each time. That fraction makes log wealth grow fastest over many bets.
screens.question: With £10,000 of capital, how much does the Kelly rule stake?

hints.text: Work out $2p - 1$ first.
Here $p = 0.6$.

feedback.correct: Kelly stakes a fifth of capital.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the capital by $2p - 1$.

byKey.p: You staked $p$ of your capital. Kelly stakes $2p - 1$, the edge: 0.2.
byKey.all: Staking everything risks ruin on a 40% loss. Kelly stakes $2p - 1 = 0.2$.
byKey.edge: You used $p - 0.5 = 0.1$. Kelly for an even-money bet is $p - (1 - p) = 0.2$.

explain.text: $f = 2 \times 0.6 - 1 = 0.2$, so £2,000. If the true chance out of sample is only 0.55, Kelly is 0.1. An overstated posterior means betting double what the edge supports.

screens.prose: Up days are 55% of days. Today the signal flashes (likelihood ratio 1.5). An analyst also calls “up”: she makes that call on 70% of up days and 30% of down days, independently of the signal.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

hints.text: Find the analyst’s likelihood ratio, then multiply both into the prior odds.
The analyst’s ratio is $\tfrac{0.7}{0.3} \approx 2.333$.
Odds $\tfrac{11}{9} \times 1.5 \times \tfrac{7}{3} = \tfrac{77}{18} \approx 4.278$. Then $p = \tfrac{4.278}{5.278}$.

feedback.correct: Two independent pieces of evidence on a 55% base rate give about 0.81.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by both likelihood ratios, then convert.

byKey.signal: That uses the signal alone. Multiply by the analyst’s ratio too.
byKey.analyst: That is the analyst’s 70%, taken as the chance of an up day. It is $P(\text{call} \mid \text{up})$.
byKey.no-base: You started from even odds. Up days are 55% of days, so start from odds of 11 to 9.
byKey.odds: That is the posterior odds. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{4.278}{1 + 4.278}$.

explain.text: Odds $\tfrac{55}{45} \times 1.5 \times \tfrac{7}{3} = \tfrac{77}{18} \approx 4.278$, so $p = \tfrac{77}{95} \approx 0.81$. This is valid only if the two are independent given the day. If the analyst watches the same signal, her call counts for much less.

ideas: A detection rate is $P(\text{flash} \mid \text{up})$. What moves your view is the likelihood ratio: detection rate over false-alarm rate.
Start from the base rate of up days, in odds, and multiply by one likelihood ratio per independent piece of evidence.
Correlated signals count as fewer, and a detection rate is worth only what survives out of sample.

formula.name: Posterior odds
formula.note: One factor per independent signal. Kelly stakes $2p - 1$ on a repeated even-money bet with known $p$.

summary.trap: Taking the detection rate as the probability of an up day.

quiz.prose: A signal has a likelihood ratio of 1.5. In a quiet market only 40% of days are up days. The signal flashes.
quiz.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

feedback.correct: Odds of 1 to 1: a coin flip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn 40% into odds, multiply by 1.5, then convert back.

byKey.prob: You multiplied the probability 0.4 by 1.5. Multiply the odds, $\tfrac{2}{3}$, instead.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the flash.

explain.text: Prior odds $\tfrac{0.4}{0.6} = \tfrac{2}{3}$. Times 1.5 gives odds of 1, so $p = 0.5$. The same flash that took a 50% prior to 60% takes a 40% prior to 50%.

quiz.prose: A research note says a signal has a “70% detection rate on up days”.
quiz.question: Which probability is that?

options.why: You took the detection rate as the probability of an up day. That needs the base rate and the false-alarm rate too.
The detection rate is a share of up days, not of all days.

feedback.correct: The detection rate is a share of up days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which group the 70% is a share of.

explain.text: “On up days, it flashed 70% of the time” conditions on the day: $P(\text{flash} \mid \text{up}) = 0.7$. To get $P(\text{up} \mid \text{flash})$ you also need how often it flashes on down days, and the base rate.

quiz.prose: A researcher tries 200 signal designs on the same ten years of data and keeps the one with the best detection rate, 62%. False alarms are 40% for all of them.
quiz.question: What should you expect of the kept signal’s detection rate on new data?

options.text: About 62%: that is what was measured
options.why: The best of 200 tries is partly luck. Selecting on the result inflates it, as with false discoveries.

options.text: Higher than 62%, as more data arrives
options.why: More data does not reward a lucky pick. The luck tends to wash out, pulling the rate down.

feedback.correct: The winner of many tries regresses on new data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how much of the 62% came from picking the best of 200.

explain.text: The kept signal is conditioned on having the best in-sample result, so its 62% includes luck. On new data the luck does not repeat. Size bets on the out-of-sample detection rate, not the in-sample one.

quiz.prose: Your chance of winning an even-money bet is 0.55.
quiz.question: What fraction of capital does the Kelly rule stake?

byKey.half: You used $p - 0.5$. Kelly for an even-money bet is $p - (1 - p)$.

explain.text: $f = 2 \times 0.55 - 1 = 0.1$. A 5-point edge over a coin flip supports a 10% stake.
